title: Code on Social Security: from PF to the gig worker
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A single Code for provident fund, ESI, gratuity and maternity benefit, with new provisions for gig and platform work.
body:
The **Code on Social Security, 2020** is the Labour Code that deals with what happens to a worker when she falls ill, has a child, is injured, retires or dies. It brings nine existing social security laws into one text and, for the first time in an Indian central law, writes in definitions of gig workers and platform workers. This post sets out what the Code says, what is new, where the debate lies and what BMS has asked for.

## Background: why a single Code

Indian social security grew in pieces. The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, the Employees' State Insurance Act, the Payment of Gratuity Act, the Maternity Benefit Act and the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 were each written at a different time for a different purpose. They had different coverage thresholds and different officials. The Code of 2020 gathers nine such laws together. According to the PRS Legislative Research summary, the Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 19 September 2020, passed there on 22 September and passed by the Rajya Sabha on 23 September 2020.

## What the Code covers

**Provident fund, pension and insurance.** The Code carries forward the Employees' Provident Fund, the Employees' Pension Scheme and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance scheme, run by the Central Board of Trustees. A summary of the Code notes that the provident fund applies to establishments with 20 or more employees, with employer and employee each contributing 12 per cent of wages, and that the Government can extend coverage to other establishments.

**Medical care and cash benefits.** The Employees' State Insurance scheme, run by the ESI Corporation, gives medical, sickness, maternity, disability and dependants' benefits. The summary notes it applies to establishments with ten or more employees, subject to a wage ceiling, and smaller establishments may opt in.

**Gratuity.** The general rule remains five years of continuous service, with exceptions such as death or disability. Gratuity is calculated at 15 days' wages for each completed year. The period is reduced to three years for working journalists. For fixed-term employees, the Code allows gratuity pro rata without the five-year requirement. PRS points out that the Industrial Relations Code links a fixed-term worker's gratuity to one year of service and that the two Codes are not perfectly aligned, which is something rules will have to settle.

**Maternity benefit.** The Code retains 26 weeks of paid maternity leave for the first two children, and 12 weeks from the third child. A woman who adopts a child below three months gets 12 weeks. Nursing breaks continue until the child is 15 months old, and establishments with 50 or more employees must provide a crèche.

## Gig, platform and unorganised workers

India's workforce is overwhelmingly informal, and the Code tries to bring some of those workers into a legal framework.

- A **gig worker** is one who works or earns outside the traditional employer-employee relationship.
- A **platform worker** is similar, but gets work through an online platform and is paid for the service. A food-delivery rider or a ride-hailing driver can fit the description.
- An **unorganised worker** is a home-based worker, a self-employed worker or a wage worker in the unorganised sector.

PRS notes that these categories overlap, so one person can fall under more than one definition, and it is not always clear which scheme applies. Aggregators, meaning digital platforms that connect workers to customers, are required to contribute to a social security fund for these workers. The Code sets the contribution between 1 and 2 per cent of the aggregator's annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of the amount paid or payable to gig and platform workers. The Central Government must set up a fund for these workers, and States run funds for unorganised workers. All three groups have to be registered on a designated portal, and benefits such as life and disability cover, health, old-age protection and housing can be offered through notified schemes. A National Social Security Board advises on schemes, with State Boards for the unorganised sector.

## Numbers and dates to remember

- Nine laws merged into one Code.
- 19, 22 and 23 September 2020: introduction, Lok Sabha passage and Rajya Sabha passage.
- 1 to 2 per cent of turnover: aggregator contribution band, with a 5 per cent cap on payouts to workers.
- 26 weeks: paid maternity leave for the first two children.
- 5 years, or pro rata for fixed-term workers: gratuity.

## Why it matters to workers

For decades, social security reached mainly those who worked in large, formal establishments. A construction worker, a head-load worker, a domestic worker or a delivery rider might work every day for years without a provident fund account or an insurance card. The Code's promise is wider coverage. Whether it delivers depends on three practical things: rules that define who is eligible, registration that actually reaches workers, and money that is actually collected and spent.

PRS also flags questions worth watching. Mandatory Aadhaar linking for benefits may raise privacy concerns, the overlap between worker categories may confuse scheme design, and the Code reduces some penalties and review powers compared with the older laws. These are points on which unions and workers can ask for clarity in rules.

## What BMS says

BMS supports extending social security to all workers. In its pre-Budget representation of 6 January 2025, reported by Organiser, it asked that the Code on Social Security be notified without delay, that funding be ensured for the unorganised sector and for boards such as those for beedi workers and contract labour, which were earlier financed through a cess, and that special packages be considered for sectors such as plantation, beedi, agriculture, fisheries and platform-economy workers. It also asked for recognition of ASHA, Anganwadi, NHM and mid-day meal workers as workers, and for Ayushman Bharat benefits to be extended to pensioners under the Employees' Pension Scheme. Over the years BMS has also argued for registration of all unorganised workers, portable benefits that move with the worker and a statutory board and fund for each occupational group.

## What remains to be done

The Code is a framework. Rules must say who is covered, at what wage ceiling and with what proof. Platforms and workers must be registered. Funds must be built and spent transparently. State Governments have to constitute their Boards. And contract and fixed-term workers must be able to claim benefits in practice and not only on paper. We return to gig and platform workers in a later post.

## A later update

The Ministry of Labour and Employment announced that the four Labour Codes would come into effect on 21 November 2025. A law-firm summary says the Social Security Code is substantially in force, with some sections excluded for the time being. Readers should check the current notified Rules for the exact position.
